name: Cumulative P&L
brief:
A backtest turns a list of positions into profit and loss. The one rule that matters: a day earns what you held going into it, never what you decided at its close.

Write `cumulative_pnl(positions, prices)`. Both lists have one entry per day. `positions[t]` is the number of shares held after the close of day $t$. Return the running total of P&L for every day.
definition:
The P&L on day $t \ge 1$ is the position held into the day times the price move:

$$\text{pnl}_t = q_{t-1} \, (P_t - P_{t-1})$$

The cumulative P&L on day $t$ is the sum of $\text{pnl}_1$ to $\text{pnl}_t$, and it is 0 on day 0. Return a list as long as `prices`, or an empty list when there are no prices.
constraints: $O(n)$ time. Re-summing every day from the start is $O(n^2)$ and runs out of time on the long test.
No trading costs. Positions may be negative (short) or fractional.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Start the total at 0.0 and the output at `[0.0]`. For each later day, add `positions[t - 1] * (prices[t] - prices[t - 1])` to the total and append it.

examples.note: Holding one share: up 2, then down 1.
The 10 shares are bought at the close of day 1, so the move from 50 to 51 earns nothing.
Short 5 shares while the price falls by 2.

tests.name: Empty lists
tests.why: No prices means no days. Return an empty list.

tests.name: Single day
tests.why: The first day has no move yet, so the list is just `[0.0]`.

tests.name: Never trades
tests.why: Holding nothing earns nothing, whatever the price does.

tests.name: No look-ahead
tests.why: Day $t$ earns what you held at the close of day $t - 1$. Using `positions[t]` trades on a price you had not seen.

tests.name: Short position
tests.why: A short position gains when the price falls: $-3 \times (47 - 50) = 9$.

tests.name: Long to short
tests.why: Flip the sign of the position when it flips. Each day uses the previous close.

tests.name: Fractional shares
tests.why: Positions can be fractions. Multiply, do not round.

tests.name: Daily closes
tests.why: Keep a running total and append it every day, starting with 0.0 on the first day.

tests.name: Long series, final total
tests.note: 100,000 days of a seeded random walk and changing positions
tests.why: This test has 100,000 days. Re-summing from the start each day takes about $5 \times 10^9$ steps; a running total takes $10^5$.

tests.name: Long series, length
tests.why: Return one total per day, including the 0.0 on the first day.

how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests, the last on 100,000 days. Lists are compared element by element, and each float counts when it is within a relative 1e-9 of the expected value.
where: Builds toward 1.1 level 3, time series in pandas, and the backtests of topic 2.5.
notes: `positions[t - 1]` is what you held through day $t$. Using `positions[t]` is look-ahead bias: it trades on a close you had not seen.
A running `total` adds one day at a time, so the whole list costs $O(n)$.
prelude:
def _walk(n, seed, start, step):
    # Seeded random walk from an integer LCG, so every Python makes the same prices
    x = seed
    p = start
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648
        p = p * (1 + step * ((x % 2001 - 1000) / 1000))
        out.append(p)
    return out
